article.title: Richard Wolff on Becoming an American Marxist
article.author: Sharon Kyle, Dick Price
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. The best education Richard Wolff got at Harvard, he told us, began when a man knocked on his dorm-room door. Fritz Pappenheim, a scholar who had served the Spanish Republican government during the civil war, had fled to France after Franco’s victory. Wolff’s father, an old friend, helped him get papers to stay in Paris and later a visa to come to the United States. Years later, Pappenheim found a way to repay him. He offered to teach his son to read Marx in German. The arrangement was simple. Every couple of weeks, the Harvard freshman would come over for dinner and French wine. Pappenheim would find Marxist writings on whatever Wolff was studying, and the two would talk through the readings. Wolff could then bring both sets of work to his papers on subjects like the French Revolution and World War I. His professors gave him high marks. They seemed to think the insights were his own, he recalled. For four years, Wolff had two educations running side by side. The one that would shape his life began with an invitation to read what his professors left out. His father would later urge him to stay in school and earn the credentials that, in his view, could protect a young radical. Wolff came to appreciate the advice. Degrees from Harvard, Stanford and Yale gave him room to teach ideas that had once been risky even to discuss at school. That story is part of Question Everything: Professor Richard Wolff on Becoming an American Marxist , a book-length conversation with his former student Ian Seda-Irizarry, now an economics professor at John Jay College. The two started meeting over Zoom during the pandemic, working through Wolff’s family history, his education and the ways his teaching and political work shaped each other. Democracy at Work announced a December 7 release. Related: Beyond Trump: Why Democrats Need a New New Deal for Working Americans Who gets the fruits of the labor? When we asked Wolff where a Marxist starts in looking at any economy, he began with a question anybody who has held a job can ask. “Who gets the fruits of the labor of the people doing work?” Consider the example he gave us. A blouse manufacturer offers you $25 an hour. The company expects your work to add more than $25 an hour in value, whether you help make more blouses or improve the ones it sells. In Wolff’s explanation of Marx, the difference between the value workers add and what they receive in wages is the surplus. Workers produce it. Owners decide how to use it. The money can go toward expanding the business, buying new equipment or rewarding investors. What interests Wolff is who gets to make those decisions. The people who put in the hours have to live on their wages, while the people who control the surplus can use it to increase their wealth and extend their influence. That’s where workplace democracy comes in. Wolff asked us to imagine a restaurant or factory run on the principle of one worker, one vote. The people who do the work would decide together what to produce, what technology to use, where to operate and how to distribute what’s left after paying the bills. In a restaurant, that might mean deciding together whether to replace aging equipment, raise pay or put money aside for a slow season. The people who live with those decisions would have a vote in making them. Related: China and the US: Meeting Is Good, Agreement Is Better How racial division creates a foothold Sharon asked what happens when politicians persuade the public that a racialized group deserves fewer rights or less protection. Can elites use that acceptance as a foothold to hold down wages, limit political participation and accumulate more power? Wolff answered with the example of an undocumented construction worker. A boss can withhold a paycheck knowing that the worker may be afraid to report the theft for fear of deportation. The boss gains leverage from that fear. Then politicians can encourage other workers, who are also struggling to get by, to blame immigrants for low wages or deteriorating public services. The employer’s power gets less scrutiny, and people who might have made common cause are encouraged to see each other as the problem. Wolff pointed to Donald Trump’s use of the word “invasion” for migration across the southern border. Describing people who have left their homes and families as an invading army makes it easier for the public to accept their mistreatment. For Sharon, this is where the foothold matters. Once the public accepts weaker protections for one group, employers can turn that vulnerability into leverage at work, and political leaders can use the divisions it creates to make a broader challenge to their power harder to mount. The people targeted bear the immediate harm. The division weakens the bargaining position of workers who might otherwise stand together. For Wolff, the subject is personal. His parents fled Europe, and members of both sides of his family were killed in the Holocaust. In the United States, his father’s credentials as a lawyer and judge went unrecognized. The Quakers helped him find work, and by the time Richard was born in Youngstown, Ohio, his father was supplementing his teaching income by pushing a wheelbarrow at Youngstown Sheet and Tube. Richard grew up speaking German and some French and learned English when he went to kindergarten. Related: From Welfare State to Warfare State: Europe’s Dangerous Turn What a fight for reform can teach Dick asked how incremental reforms might add up to structural change, taking New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani as an example. Wolff pointed to stronger rent protections and city-run grocery stores in underserved neighborhoods as reforms that could improve people’s lives. He was equally interested in what happens when people organize for those changes and encounter the limits of what officials can deliver. Both Sharon and Wolff came back to campaign finance. An elected official who depends on wealthy donors has to consider what those donors will do when a policy threatens their interests. Wolff saw a different source of political power in Mamdani’s campaign. People gave $10 or $20, sometimes more than once, and volunteers kept showing up at voters’ doors. Canvassers knocked at Wolff’s own apartment four times, he recalled. Nobody came by for any other candidate. Winning an election gives that kind of organization a chance to change policy. The fights that follow can show people where power still sits and what they would have to organize to change. For Wolff, that is how a campaign over rents or groceries can lead to a larger fight about who makes the decisions that shape a city. Wolff told us that his father once asked him to help take books about socialism off the family shelves. They put them into boxes in the basement and covered the boxes with blankets. His father was curious about those ideas and afraid of what could happen if a neighbor saw them. Years later, Pappenheim put some of those ideas back within reach. Wolff has spent his career doing the same for students and for listeners of Economic Update . As he put it to us, “Being a teacher made me a better political activist.” He credits his activism with making him a better teacher, too. The question his teaching leaves with us is one we can take into a workplace, an election or a fight over rents. Who gets to decide, and what would it take for the people who live with the decision to have a say?
